lead: A beam twists when a load acts off its axis: an edge beam carrying a cantilever slab or a canopy, a curved balcony beam, a lintel under a sunshade. The twisting moment T<sub>u</sub> sets up shear stress that circulates round the section, so one side face sees bending shear plus torsion shear. After cracking the torque is carried by a cage of closed stirrups and corner bars, with the concrete between spiral cracks acting as struts. IS 456 does not ask for this space truss to be analysed. It turns T<sub>u</sub> into an equivalent shear for the stirrups and an equivalent moment for the longitudinal bars, so the familiar shear and flexure checks do the work.
prereq: You need: τv, τc and τc,max from Behaviour of RC beams in shear and the stirrup formula from Design of shear reinforcement.

blocks.text: Equilibrium torsion is torque the member must carry to keep the structure standing. An edge beam holding a cantilever canopy is the classic case: if the beam could not resist the twist, the canopy would fall. IS 456 requires such members to be designed for the full torque.

Compatibility torsion comes only because members are cast together. A secondary beam framing into a main beam rotates at its end and twists the main beam, but if the main beam cracked and softened in torsion, the secondary beam would simply carry its load as a simply supported beam. IS 456 says no specific design for torsion is needed in such indeterminate cases, provided the torsional stiffness is neglected when the internal forces are calculated; the shear reinforcement is taken to control the torsional cracking.
The exam test: release the twist in your mind. If the structure still stands, it is compatibility torsion; if something collapses, it is equilibrium torsion.

In an uncracked solid rectangle the torsional shear stress is zero at the centre and largest at the middle of the long faces. It acts in a closed loop round the section. On one side face it adds to the bending shear stress; on the opposite face it subtracts. The principal tension is at 45° on every face, so the cracks wind round the beam as a spiral.

After cracking, the inside of the section does little. The torque is carried by a thin outer tube, modelled as a space truss: closed stirrups are the hoops, longitudinal bars at the corners are the stringers, and the concrete between the spiral cracks forms struts at about 45°. Two facts follow. Torsion needs transverse steel and longitudinal steel together, and the stirrups must be closed, because the shear flow runs round all four faces. An open U stirrup has no top leg to carry it.

A beam under bending and torsion can also fail by skew bending: a spiral crack on three faces and crushing along the fourth. This is why IS 456 adds a torsion term to the bending moment, and why, when the torque is large, steel is needed on the compression face too.
V<sub>e</sub> = V<sub>u</sub> + 1.6 T<sub>u</sub>/b     τ<sub>ve</sub> = V<sub>e</sub>/(b d) ≤ τ<sub>c,max</sub>
blocks.where: V<sub>e</sub> is the equivalent shear (N); V<sub>u</sub> the factored shear (N); T<sub>u</sub> the factored torque (N·mm); b the breadth (mm); τ<sub>ve</sub> the equivalent shear stress (N/mm²); d the effective depth (mm). With T<sub>u</sub> in kN·m and b in m, 1.6 T<sub>u</sub>/b comes out in kN.

blocks.text: If τ<sub>ve</sub> exceeds τ<sub>c,max</sub>, the section must be enlarged. If τ<sub>ve</sub> ≤ τ<sub>c</sub>, minimum shear reinforcement is enough. If τ<sub>ve</sub> > τ<sub>c</sub>, both longitudinal and transverse torsion steel are designed.

A<sub>sv</sub> = T<sub>u</sub> s<sub>v</sub>/(b<sub>1</sub> d<sub>1</sub> × 0.87 f<sub>y</sub>) + V<sub>u</sub> s<sub>v</sub>/(2.5 d<sub>1</sub> × 0.87 f<sub>y</sub>)
but not less than (τ<sub>ve</sub> − τ<sub>c</sub>) b s<sub>v</sub>/(0.87 f<sub>y</sub>)
blocks.where: A<sub>sv</sub> is the area of the two legs of a closed stirrup (mm²); s<sub>v</sub> its spacing (mm); b<sub>1</sub> and d<sub>1</sub> the centre-to-centre distances between the corner bars across the width and the depth (mm).

blocks.text: M<sub>t</sub> = T<sub>u</sub> (1 + D/b)/1.7     M<sub>e1</sub> = M<sub>u</sub> + M<sub>t</sub>     M<sub>e2</sub> = M<sub>t</sub> − M<sub>u</sub> (if M<sub>t</sub> > M<sub>u</sub>)
blocks.where: Mt is the equivalent moment from torsion; Mu the factored moment; D the overall depth, so D/b has no unit; Me1 is designed on the flexural tension face, Me2 on the compression face (see Combined bending, shear and torsion).

items: Spacing of torsion stirrups: not more than x<sub>1</sub>, (x<sub>1</sub> + y<sub>1</sub>)/4 and 300 mm, where x<sub>1</sub> and y<sub>1</sub> are the short and long dimensions of the stirrup.
At least one longitudinal bar in each corner of the stirrups, and extra side bars when a dimension exceeds 450 mm.
Stirrups closed, with ends anchored by 135° hooks round a corner bar.

examples.question: An edge beam 300 mm × 600 mm (d = 550 mm) carries a factored shear V<sub>u</sub> = 120 kN and a factored torque T<sub>u</sub> = 30 kN·m from a cantilever canopy. Concrete is M25 and steel Fe415. The bottom steel is four 20 mm bars (p<sub>t</sub> = 0.76 %); top corner bars are 12 mm; nominal cover is 30 mm and the stirrups are 10 mm. Check the section and design the closed stirrups.
steps: The canopy would fall if the beam could twist freely, so this is equilibrium torsion.
V<sub>e</sub> = 120 + 1.6 × 30/0.3 = 280 kN; τ<sub>ve</sub> = 280 × 10³/(300 × 550) = 1.70 N/mm² < τ<sub>c,max</sub> = 3.1 N/mm², so the section is adequate.
Table 19, M25, p<sub>t</sub> = 0.76 %: τ<sub>c</sub> = 0.57 N/mm². Since τ<sub>ve</sub> > τ<sub>c</sub>, torsion steel is needed.
Corner bar centres are 30 + 10 + 10 = 50 mm (bottom) and 30 + 10 + 6 = 46 mm (top) from the faces, so b<sub>1</sub> = 300 − 100 = 200 mm and d<sub>1</sub> = 600 − 50 − 46 = 504 mm.
Two-legged 10 mm stirrups: A<sub>sv</sub> = 157.1 mm², so 0.87 f<sub>y</sub> A<sub>sv</sub> = 0.87 × 415 × 157.1 = 56,720 N.
Lower limit: s<sub>v</sub> ≤ 56,720/((1.697 − 0.57) × 300) = 167.8 mm, with the unrounded τ<sub>ve</sub> = 1.697 N/mm².
Spacing limits: stirrup centreline 230 mm × 530 mm, so x<sub>1</sub> = 230, (x<sub>1</sub> + y<sub>1</sub>)/4 = 190 and 300 mm. The strength value governs: provide 10 mm closed stirrups at 140 mm.
examples.answer: V<sub>e</sub> = 280 kN, τ<sub>ve</sub> = 1.70 N/mm² (below 3.1, above τ<sub>c</sub> = 0.57); two-legged 10 mm closed stirrups at 140 mm centres (strength needs 144.4 mm; the other limits are 167.8, 190, 230 and 300 mm).

traps: Using open U stirrups for torsion. The shear flow goes round all four faces, so the stirrups must be closed and hooked round a corner bar.

Mixing units in V<sub>e</sub> = V<sub>u</sub> + 1.6 T<sub>u</sub>/b. With T<sub>u</sub> = 30 kN·m and b = 0.3 m the term is 160 kN; with b written as 300 it is 0.16, which is wrong unless T<sub>u</sub> is in kN·mm.
Taking b<sub>1</sub> and d<sub>1</sub> as the beam size. They are the distances between the centres of the corner bars: 200 mm and 504 mm here, not 300 and 600 mm.
Designing compatibility torsion as if it were equilibrium torsion, or the reverse. Ask whether the structure would still stand if the member could twist freely.
Designing the stirrups and forgetting that torsion also needs longitudinal steel (M<sub>t</sub> added to M<sub>u</sub>).

quiz.q: Write the IS 456 expressions for V<sub>e</sub> and M<sub>t</sub> and name every symbol.
quiz.a: V<sub>e</sub> = V<sub>u</sub> + 1.6 T<sub>u</sub>/b and M<sub>t</sub> = T<sub>u</sub> (1 + D/b)/1.7, where V<sub>u</sub> is the factored shear, T<sub>u</sub> the factored torque, b the breadth and D the overall depth of the beam.

quiz.q: Explain the difference between equilibrium torsion and compatibility torsion with one example each.
quiz.a: Equilibrium torsion is needed to keep the structure in equilibrium, for example an edge beam supporting a cantilever canopy. Compatibility torsion arises only from the members being monolithic, for example a main beam twisted by a secondary beam framing into it; it can be neglected if torsional stiffness is ignored in the analysis.

quiz.q: Why must torsion reinforcement include both closed stirrups and longitudinal bars?
quiz.a: After cracking the torque is carried by a space truss: the spiral concrete struts push on the corners, closed stirrups act as hoops and the longitudinal bars as stringers. Without either one the truss cannot be in equilibrium.

quiz.q: b = 250 mm, D = 500 mm, d = 460 mm, V<sub>u</sub> = 80 kN, T<sub>u</sub> = 20 kN·m, M25. Find V<sub>e</sub> and τ<sub>ve</sub> and check the section.
quiz.a: V<sub>e</sub> = 80 + 1.6 × 20/0.25 = 80 + 128 = 208 kN. τ<sub>ve</sub> = 208 × 10³/(250 × 460) = 1.81 N/mm² < 3.1 N/mm², so the section is adequate.

quiz.q: In the worked example, what A<sub>sv</sub> is needed if the stirrups are placed at 140 mm?
A designer gets τ<sub>ve</sub> = 3.4 N/mm² for an M25 beam and adds closer stirrups. Comment.
quiz.a: τ<sub>ve</sub> exceeds τ<sub>c,max</sub> = 3.1 N/mm², so the concrete struts would crush whatever the stirrups. The fix is a bigger section (b or D) or a higher grade, after which the torsion steel is designed again.

beyond: Not for the exam. Eurocode 2 and the ACI code design torsion with the thin-walled tube and space truss model directly, giving the stirrup area and the longitudinal steel from the area enclosed by the shear flow. Box girders of curved flyovers are designed this way, and their torsional stiffness matters for how the deck shares load. Research on the softened truss model explains why concrete struts crush at a lower stress when they are cracked across. Search for 'thin-walled tube analogy', 'softened truss model' and 'torsion in curved box girders'.
